passage: A survey of the basin published in 1908 called the flights of terraces cut into its walls ______, and the label held for eighty years. Each bench was read as a stand of the vanished lake, cut while the water paused at one level long enough to bite into the rock. Radiocarbon ages from the terrace gravels now fall in no order: the highest bench is younger than two of the benches beneath it, and one bench has yielded two ages a thousand years apart.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: successive
coeval
conjectural
unremarkable
correct_answer: successive
explanation: The reading the label carried is that each bench records a separate pause of the lake at a lower level than the last, which is to say the flight is "successive": one bench after another in time as well as in height. "Coeval" is the sharpest wrong answer because the scrambled ages do loosen the tie between height and date, but a bench that is younger than two benches below it is not contemporaneous with them, and the passage reports disorder rather than simultaneity. "Conjectural" describes the standing of the 1908 reading as the last sentence leaves it, not the property the survey attributed to the terraces themselves. And "unremarkable" is contradicted by the survey's own interest in the flights, which it took the trouble to name and interpret.

passage: Ore geologists once treated tourmaline in a granite as a ______ sign of a buried tin vein, and crews were sent into the field on nothing more. The reasoning was sound as far as it went: tourmaline crystallizes where boron-rich fluid moves through cooling rock, and that same fluid carries tin. But the fluid travels for kilometers and lays down tourmaline along its whole path, while the tin drops out only in the short stretch where the temperature falls fastest.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ubiquitous
dispositive
premonitory
contested
correct_answer: dispositive
explanation: Crews were dispatched on the strength of the mineral alone, so the sign was treated as settling the question rather than merely raising it, which is what "dispositive" says. "Ubiquitous" is the strongest trap because the passage does establish that tourmaline is laid down along the fluid's whole path, but that is the fact which undoes the old practice, not the property that justified it. "Contested" reverses the sentence, which reports a view geologists acted on without argument. And "premonitory" would make the mineral a warning of something still to come, whereas the vein it is supposed to indicate is already in the ground, laid down by the same fluid on the same passage.

passage: Historians of the printed book long described the first roman types as ______, on the reasoning that a punchcutter who had spent his working life among manuscripts would cut the letters his hand already knew. The comparison does not survive measurement. The capitals of the 1460s are built from a compass and a straightedge, and their proportions repeat those of carved inscriptions that no scribe of that century had been trained to write.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: improvised
austere
derivative
vernacular
correct_answer: derivative
explanation: The historians' reasoning is that the punchcutter reproduced forms he had inherited from manuscript practice, so the types were held to be "derivative": taken from a source rather than devised. "Vernacular" is the most tempting alternative, since the letters a scribe knew are indeed the ordinary letters of his own place and trade, but the word names where a form comes from socially rather than the relation of copy to model that the reasoning turns on, and the corrective sentence answers the charge of copying, not of ordinariness. "Improvised" is the opposite of what the reasoning alleges, which is that nothing was invented. And "austere" describes an appearance the passage never discusses; compass construction is offered as evidence of a source, not of plainness.

passage: A specimen sheet issued by one foundry in 1734 lists forty-one sizes of a single face, which sounds like abundance and was nothing of the kind. The matrices had been struck by four hands over sixty years, and the sizes form no series: two of them differ by less than a hair, and between two others there is a gap wide enough to swallow three more. The sheet recorded ______ rather than a system.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: an exaggeration
an abbreviation
a facsimile
an accumulation
correct_answer: an accumulation
explanation: The forty-one sizes were gathered over six decades from four unrelated hands and were never designed against one another, so the sheet recorded "an accumulation": what had piled up rather than what had been planned. "An exaggeration" would require the count to be inflated, and the passage never questions that forty-one sets of matrices existed. "An abbreviation" points the wrong way, since the complaint is that the list is larger and less orderly than a designed series, not shorter than one. And "a facsimile" would make the sheet a copy of something, which nothing in the text suggests.

passage: Ravens that watch a rival hide food will go to the cache once the rival has left, and for years this was reported plainly as theft by memory. Later trials made that account ______. A raven that has merely seen the site from across the aviary performs at chance, while a raven that watched the hiding through a peephole, itself unseen, goes straight to the spot and digs. The bird is tracking not only where the food went but whether it was watched going there.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unwarranted
incomplete
circular
premature
correct_answer: incomplete
explanation: The trials leave the raiding behavior exactly where it was and add a condition the old account said nothing about, so they made that account "incomplete": true so far as it went and short of the facts. "Unwarranted" is the closest miss and is too strong, since the birds do return to caches they have seen filled and memory is doing part of the work the old description credited it with. "Circular" would charge the account with assuming what it set out to show, and no such defect is described. And "premature" concerns when a claim was made rather than what it left out; the passage faults the content of the description, not its timing.

passage: Cleaner wrasse pass the mark test, scraping at a colored spot that is visible to them only in a mirror, and the finding is usually reported as a small-scale version of the primate result. The fish's behavior is ______ all the same. It scrapes its throat against the sand and then swims back to the mirror to look again, a sequence no primate performs and no account of the animal's ecology predicts.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: idiosyncratic
inconsequential
derivative
equivocal
correct_answer: idiosyncratic
explanation: The wrasse does something no primate does and nothing in its own natural history anticipates, which makes the behavior "idiosyncratic": particular to this animal rather than an instance of a general pattern. "Derivative" states the very comparison the sentence is set against, since the point is that the sequence resembles nothing else. "Equivocal" would mean the behavior admits of two readings, and the passage reports the sequence as clearly observed rather than ambiguous. And "inconsequential" is refused by the passage, which presents the unpredicted sequence as the very thing that makes the finding worth a second look.

passage: Under prior appropriation the senior right holder may call the river, obliging junior users upstream to close their headgates. In practice the call is ______. It is made perhaps twice a decade on most western streams, and a watermaster asked to enforce one will spend the first week persuading juniors to yield without an order. The right itself is not weak; it is simply expensive to exercise, and seniors save it for the years in which nothing else will do.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: nominal
discretionary
contentious
latent
correct_answer: latent
explanation: The call is available at any time and almost never used, which is what "latent" names: a power held in reserve rather than one exercised or lost. "Nominal" is the strongest distractor and is refused by the passage in as many words, since a nominal right is one that exists in name only and the text says the right "is not weak." "Discretionary" would locate the choice with the official, and the passage puts the reluctance in the watermaster's practice while leaving the entitlement with the senior. And "contentious" describes disputes the text does not report; the juniors in the passage are persuaded rather than fought.

passage: The compact of 1922 divided the river between an upper and a lower group of states using an annual flow figure the negotiators took to be ______. The gauge record available to them then ran to eighteen years. Tree rings have since placed those eighteen years among the wettest of the past five centuries, and in no decade since the signing has the river carried the quantity the compact apportions.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: provisional
generous
representative
incontrovertible
correct_answer: representative
explanation: The negotiators divided a fixed quantity on the assumption that their short record stood for the river's ordinary behavior, so they took the figure to be "representative": a fair sample of the whole. "Generous" describes what the figure turned out to be and is the reading the tree rings supply, not the one the negotiators held when they used it. "Provisional" would mean they expected to revise it, and a compact that apportions a fixed quantity treats the number as settled. And "incontrovertible" overshoots: what the negotiators needed was a figure typical of the river, not one beyond challenge, and nothing in the text says they thought the number could not be questioned.

passage: Seismic tomography shows a slab of old ocean floor lying flat at the base of the mantle beneath one continent, and the depth is read as the record of a subduction that ended a hundred million years ago. Turning a depth into a date requires a sinking rate, and the sinking rate is not measured but assumed. Published estimates of it differ by a factor of two, which puts the end of subduction anywhere in a window fifty million years wide. The slab is there regardless, and no other process is known to place a cold sheet at that depth.
prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It supplies the sinking rate that the previous sentence reports to be missing.
It withdraws the claim that the slab is a piece of subducted ocean floor.
It grants a margin of error to the date announced in the text's opening sentence.
It explains why tomography renders the slab as a flat sheet rather than a plume.
correct_answer: It grants a margin of error to the date announced in the text's opening sentence.
explanation: The opening sentence puts a date on the end of subduction; the third sentence measures how loosely that date is fixed, so it "grants a margin of error to the date announced in the text's opening sentence." It does not "supply the sinking rate that the previous sentence reports to be missing": what it supplies is the spread among competing estimates, which is the absence of a settled rate rather than its provision. It does not "withdraw the claim that the slab is a piece of subducted ocean floor," a claim the final sentence goes out of its way to keep. And it does not "explain why tomography renders the slab as a flat sheet rather than a plume"; the flatness is stated in the first sentence and is never accounted for anywhere in the text.

passage: The linotype is generally credited with making the daily newspaper thick. The credit has a mechanism behind it: a machine that cast a whole line at one stroke cut the cost of composition by about four fifths, and papers did grow in the decade after it spread. The news columns grew by a tenth.
prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It reports a common credit, disputes the cost saving on which it rests, and offers a rival cause for the paper's growth.
It describes a machine, measures its effect on reporting, and predicts the decline of the daily paper.
It sets out two explanations of a change in newspapers and rejects the one more usually preferred.
It reports a common credit, allows the mechanism behind it, and then confines the effect to one part of the paper.
correct_answer: It reports a common credit, allows the mechanism behind it, and then confines the effect to one part of the paper.
explanation: The text credits the linotype, endorses the cost argument that supports the credit, and then shows that the growth landed almost entirely in advertising, which is the sequence in "it reports a common credit, allows the mechanism behind it, and then confines the effect to one part of the paper." The option that has the text "dispute the cost saving on which it rests" is right about the first and third moves and wrong about the middle one, which is the load-bearing difference: the four-fifths saving is asserted by the text, not challenged. Nothing here "predicts the decline of the daily paper," and the only measurement of reporting is the tenth in the last sentence, offered as a limit rather than as the subject. And the text "sets out two explanations" of nothing; one account is given and then bounded.

passage: A crow of one island species will bend a straight length of wire into a hook to lift a bucket from a tube, and the demonstration is famous. Less often reported is that this bird had watched a person bend wire on eleven earlier days, on a task that was not this one. Birds given no such exposure bend nothing: they probe with the wire straight, then stop. The species does make hooks in the wild, from the stems of a plant that are already curved.
prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

It supplies the exposure that the text's second sentence identifies as necessary to the feat.
It concedes that wild birds solve the bucket task without any instruction.
It explains why birds given no exposure probe with the wire held straight.
correct_answer: It names a natural behavior that resembles the demonstration without accounting for it.
explanation: The wild hook-making is close enough to the laboratory feat to be worth mentioning and does not explain it, since the wild stems arrive curved and the wire does not, so the sentence "names a natural behavior that resembles the demonstration without accounting for it." The claim that it "supplies the exposure that the text's second sentence identifies as necessary to the feat" describes something the text really does contain, but in the second sentence: eleven days of watching a person, not a plant. It does not "concede that wild birds solve the bucket task without any instruction"; no wild bird in the text meets a bucket, and the curved stems require no bending. And it does not "explain why birds given no exposure probe with the wire held straight," a result the third sentence reports and the text nowhere accounts for.

passage: A state that recognizes instream flow rights can hold water in the channel for fish without anyone diverting it, and eleven states now do. Such a right takes its place in the ordinary seniority queue, which means one filed in 1980 yields to a ditch filed in 1890, and in a dry year yields altogether. The only way to put genuinely senior water in the channel is to buy an old right and convert it, and old rights are expensive. On three rivers it has been done, and those flows held through two droughts.

choices: It reports the outcome of the three conversions the text goes on to describe.
It concedes a limit on the instrument the first sentence introduces.
It explains why buying an old right costs as much as the text says it does.
It disputes the claim that eleven states hold water in the channel.
correct_answer: It concedes a limit on the instrument the first sentence introduces.
explanation: The first sentence presents instream rights as a working tool; the second says what the tool cannot do, in the year when it would matter most, so it "concedes a limit on the instrument the first sentence introduces." It does not "report the outcome of the three conversions the text goes on to describe"; that outcome is the last sentence, and it is favorable, while this sentence is not. It does not "explain why buying an old right costs as much as the text says it does": the expense is asserted in the third sentence and never traced to seniority or to anything else. And it does not "dispute the claim that eleven states hold water in the channel," which the text states without qualification and never takes back.

passage: Ripple marks preserved in sandstone are read as the record of a shallow sea, and in most outcrops the reading is safe. The formation described here is a hundred meters thick and ripple-marked from bottom to top. A shallow sea does not stay shallow as it fills, so if the water remained shallow while a hundred meters of sand came in, the floor beneath it must have been sinking at very nearly the rate of deposition. That is the whole interest of the outcrop, and the match is not a coincidence: the sinking is what made the room.
prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text?
choices: It questions whether ripple marks record a shallow sea at all.
It reports the measurement that the text's closing sentence goes on to explain.
It concedes that the match described at the end of the text cannot be accounted for.
It draws out what the formation's thickness requires the sea floor to have done.
correct_answer: It draws out what the formation's thickness requires the sea floor to have done.
explanation: The sentence takes the thickness from the preceding sentence and the shallow-water reading from the first, and derives a consequence about the floor, so it "draws out what the formation's thickness requires the sea floor to have done." It does not "question whether ripple marks record a shallow sea at all"; the reading is granted in the first sentence and used here as a premise. It does not "report the measurement that the text's closing sentence goes on to explain": the measurement is the hundred meters given in the second sentence, and this sentence reasons from it. passage: Legibility is nearly always tested by flashing single letters and asking readers to name them, and the faces that win such tests are those whose letters differ most from one another. Continuous reading does not proceed letter by letter. The eye takes in a word's outline and fixates four or five times a second, and outlines are made by ascenders and descenders rather than by the features that separate an n from an h. It does not follow that the flash test measures nothing. It measures something continuous reading calls on only when the outline fails.

They withdraw the objection raised against the flash test earlier in the text.
They restrict the scope of that objection rather than withdrawing it.
They grant that the flash test measures nothing while defending its convenience.

The reading that they "withdraw the objection raised against the flash test earlier in the text" is the one serious competitor and turns on a single word: the text says the test measures something, not that the earlier criticism was mistaken, and the criticism survives everywhere the outline holds. They do not "grant that the flash test measures nothing," which is the proposition the fourth sentence explicitly denies, and convenience is never mentioned. And they do not "introduce the evidence behind the text's opening claim"; the opening claim describes a testing practice, and these sentences appraise it.

passage: Honeybees returning from a rich patch dance on the comb, and the dance encodes distance and direction. For decades the open question was whether the recruits use it. Bees were trained to a feeder and recruits were tracked by radar: most flew the vector the dance gave, then searched. Recruits kept from following a dance found the feeder as well, more slowly and by odor. The dance is neither necessary nor useless, and only an experiment that took it away could have shown as much.
prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

It describes a signal, poses a question about its use, reports two results, and states a conclusion neither result alone would support.

explanation: The text introduces the dance, asks whether recruits use it, gives the tracked flights and then the deprived recruits, and closes on a verdict that needs both, which is what "reports two results, and states a conclusion neither result alone would support" captures. The option reporting "an experiment establishing its necessity" is contradicted by the fourth sentence, in which deprived recruits still arrive, and nothing in the text proposes further work. And it does not "concede that its meaning is unknown," since the first sentence states what the dance encodes, and radar is what made the tracking possible rather than what failed.

passage: Groundwater and the river beside it are one body of water, and a well within a mile of the channel takes water from the river inside a single season. The law long treated the two as separate, and the treatment was not simple ignorance: the models needed to route a pumping effect back to the channel did not exist before the 1960s, and a rule nobody can administer is not a rule. Once the models arrived, several states integrated the two systems. The wells drilled under the old regime were by then senior to most of the surface rights they draw down.
prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It defends the old rule on grounds of administrability while granting that it was hydrologically false.
It explains why wells drilled under the old regime now hold senior rights.
It concedes that the law's treatment of the two systems was an error, though an understandable one at the time.
It introduces the models that the text's third sentence reports as unavailable.
correct_answer: It defends the old rule on grounds of administrability while granting that it was hydrologically false.
explanation: The sentence agrees that the separation misdescribed the water and argues that no other rule could have been enforced before the models existed, so it "defends the old rule on grounds of administrability while granting that it was hydrologically false." The nearest miss says it "concedes that the law's treatment of the two systems was an error, though an understandable one at the time": it concedes the falsity but not the error, and the difference is the sentence's point, since a rule that cannot be administered is said not to be a rule at all rather than a bad one. It does not "explain why wells drilled under the old regime now hold senior rights"; that seniority is the last sentence's observation, and the second sentence never mentions priority. And it does not "introduce the models that the text's third sentence reports as unavailable," which inverts the order: their absence is this sentence's premise and their arrival is the third sentence's news.

passage:
Text 1

Layers of volcanic ash are the only tie between an ice core's own count of annual layers and the calendar. Two ash layers a thousand years apart in one core match eruptions dated independently, and the layer count between them is off by eleven years. The count is therefore good to about one part in a hundred, better than any competing chronology of the period.

Text 2

The eleven-year discrepancy is real, and it is the sum of errors that do not accrue at a steady rate. Layer counting fails wherever summer melt has smoothed the seasonal signal, and the smoothed stretches are not spread evenly down the core; they cluster in warm intervals. Across the warm centuries the count may be wrong by thirty years, and across the cold ones by almost none.

choices: By accepting the overall figure while denying that the error is spread evenly through the record.
By granting the eleven-year total but attributing all of it to the smoothing of summer layers.
By arguing that the two ash layers were themselves dated from the core rather than independently.
By maintaining that a layer count cannot be calibrated against eruptions at all.
correct_answer: By accepting the overall figure while denying that the error is spread evenly through the record.
explanation: Text 2 opens by conceding that the eleven years are real and spends the rest of its space showing that the error is concentrated in the warm intervals, so its response is "accepting the overall figure while denying that the error is spread evenly through the record." The option that has it "granting the eleven-year total but attributing all of it to the smoothing of summer layers" gets the concession right and overstates the rest: Text 2 says the total is a sum of unevenly accruing errors, and assigning the whole of it to melt would make the count uniformly bad rather than good in the cold centuries, which Text 2 explicitly affirms. Text 2 never questions the eruption dates, so it is not "arguing that the two ash layers were themselves dated from the core." And it is not "maintaining that a layer count cannot be calibrated against eruptions at all," since its own thirty-year and near-zero figures presuppose exactly that calibration.

passage:
Text 1

A basin closed to new appropriations still acquires new users, because an existing right may be sold and moved. Every transfer is reviewed for injury to other right holders, and the review protects them well: a right carries only its historical consumptive use to the new place, so the return flow the downstream neighbors relied on keeps arriving.

Injury review asks one question, whether another right holder is hurt. The stretch of channel between the old point of diversion and the new one loses its water outright, and a dry mile injures no right holder, because the fish in it hold no right. Nine states now allow a transfer to be reviewed for its effect on the channel as well. The rest should follow: the review already exists, and it is only its list of protected interests that is short.

By denying that a transferred right is limited to its historical consumptive use.

By accepting the dry-mile problem as real but denying that any state has yet addressed it.

explanation: Text 2 does not contest anything Text 1 says about neighbors; it ends on a prescription, that the remaining states adopt the channel review nine already have, so the response is "urging that the review's list of protected interests be widened to take in the channel." It does not object "that return flows are protected while doubting that neighbors ever relied on them," since reliance is not at issue anywhere in Text 2 and the protection is precisely what it leaves standing. It is not "denying that a transferred right is limited to its historical consumptive use"; that limit is the mechanism by which neighbors are protected and Text 2 takes no issue with it. And it cannot be "denying that any state has yet addressed it," a claim its own count of nine states refutes.
